notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0022.stoa005.opp-la: Ch. 1: 'errati canta confessio' read as 'cauta' ('careful'); the reading is uncertain. 'confessionis manus' ('the hands of confession') may be a corruption of 'munus' ('the gift/office of confession'). 'nundinat' ('puts up for sale') is a strange choice; it may mean 'exposes' or 'publicises'. Scripture references are given as printed in the edition (Ecclus. 17:20, Ezek. 18:51, Wisd. 1:16, Isa. 30:15); the usual verses are Ecclus. 17:20/24, Ezek. 18:23 and 32, Wisd. 1:13, Isa. 30:15. The edition cites Ezek. 18:51, evidently for 18:32. Ch. 2: the first sentence 'Damnum ergo in moriente experiar, qui...' does not construe ('experiar' is first person); it is translated as if it read 'experitur'. 'noa udal' is a scanning error, taken as 'non valet'. 'quae tu non quiveris publicare' and 'si non valueres silentio conscientiam' make poor sense as printed; they are taken as 'nunc quiveris' and 'si non velaveris' ('veil'). The Isaiah quotation (43:25–26) has 'non rememorabor' ('I will not remember') where modern texts have 'I will not remember your sins'. Ch. 2 also reads 'scit antequam tiam' as 'antequam facias' ('before you commit them'). Ch. 3: 'in te ante veris' is taken as 'ante fateris' ('first acknowledge'); 'ante fures' as 'ante fores' ('before the doors'); 'labo' as 'tabo' ('filth'); 'inyenuceril, tunc lalvaberi' as 'ingemueris, tunc salvaberis'. 'nodabilem' is taken as 'sanabilem' ('healing').

The text is heavily garbled by scanning; evident readings adopted include nescis for ne.cis, rudis for rus, admissum for aditurn, veluti for vetuli, fidens for fidus, inficias for insidias, unus for onus, theca for techa, teguntur for leguntur. Ch. IV: the sentence beginning 'Sed differtur interim severior poena...' is obscure ('quod latrocinii moriendi extenuaret facinus parricidii'), and the rendering is tentative. Ch. V: 'sensus tuus coeperit facti delectatione jucunditas' is corrupt; the rendering assumes a form of 'jucundari'. 'quid de Deo exigitis scelera' is taken as an address to the crimes and sins. Ch. VI: in 'a quo cum nudatur conscientia, operitur; et cum publicatur, operitur' the repeated 'operitur' may be corrupt in one place. 'De talibus spoliatum' is unclear (perhaps 'spoliatis'). 'Quomodo vult' is taken as an exclamation ('How much he wishes'). Scripture references are given as printed (Vulgate numbering), with corrected verse numbers where the printed ones are evidently misread.

Ch. VII: 'non est remissas eximere' read as 'non est permissus eximere'. 'punita est in Metere contumacia' is corrupt; the word after 'in' is unidentified and left as [...]. 'MUM coegerit' read as 'causae coegerint'. 'qai pam ane posteris teneri crimine' is garbled; read as roughly 'qui putat unius tantum teneri crimine'. 'Oagilla' read as 'flagitia' (outrages), though 'flagella' (scourges) is possible. 'non recte divisit' alludes to the Old Latin/LXX of Gen. 4:7. Ch. VIII: the sentence 'Alioquin ... abutitur; erit, enim quae ...' is scrambled in the scan; the translation follows the evident order. 'confugit ad secretarium paenitentiae': secretarium may mean a sacristy or inner chamber. Ch. IX: 'magnitudinem non contemplatus est pietate terrentis' repeats the preceding words by dittography and is translated once. 'ilL' read as 'ut'.

Several scripture references in the edition are misprinted (e.g. 'I Tim. II, 12' for 2 Tim. 2:13; 'Num. XIV, 27' for Num. 14:22; 'Jerem. III, 1' for 3:7; the Matthew and Ephesians references in ch. XIII are swapped); corrected references are given. Ch. XII: 'Fato mundi' read as 'freto mundi' (sea of the world); 'tendiculis' (snares) read for 'tenJi- colis'; 'redeundum est saburram' is awkward, perhaps corrupt ('ad saburram'?). Ch. XIII: 'menibus' read as 'mercibus'; 'aemulare priora, ut deteriora percipias' is obscure and may be corrupt. 'Peccato lenocinante' in ch. XII is odd in the merchant simile.

Ch. XIV: 'lucrificat' (of Ahab's grief for Naboth's death) gives no clear sense; rendered 'bewails' as the context requires — perhaps a corruption. 'Oagilio' read as 'flagitio', 'reum Jehitum' as 'reum debitum', 'accinxit se laceo' as 'sacco'. 'Parricidium' is used loosely for murder. Ch. XVI: 'vestigiis malum subtrahit' read as 'magis subtrahit'; 'publicans verecundiam reum pectus percussum crebro commemorat' is awkward and rendered loosely. The 'five words' are the Latin 'Deus propitius esto mihi peccatori'. Isaiah reference is printed as xxx, 25; the verse is 30:15.

Chapter XVIII: 'Curat nos Dominus non ut exteros, extraneos sibi servat...' is awkward and probably corrupt; rendered as two clauses, supplying a negative in the second. 'ad saneandum' is unintelligible; read as 'ad saltandum' (dancing), conjecturally. 'peregrinis cernebant oculis infectum' is unclear (perhaps eye-paint or foreign dyes); rendered loosely. 'vaca, diei, n"n ut torpeas' read as 'vaca Deo, non ut torpeas'. Chapter XIX: 'munimine prærepturum' is corrupt; read as 'calceamentorum' (shoes), after the Gospel. 'satisfactioni arcano' read as 'satisfactionis arcano'. Other scanning errors (e.g. 'Pomiaus' for 'Dominus', 'IItrolJique' for 'utrobique') corrected silently.

Ch. XX: the printed text of Luke 13 is jumbled by the scan ('peri-quos cecidit turris... putatisAut illi decem et octo super'); translated in the evident order 'peribitis. Aut illi decem et octo super quos cecidit turris in Siloe...'. Ch. XXI opening 'quae studio de infirmis ingemi' is corrupt; 'out of [your] infirmities' is a guess. Ch. XXII: 'congeriem' (heap) is obscure in sense; 'vorago factuorum' read as 'facinorum' (deeds/crimes). Ch. XXIII: 'urna' read as 'manus' (hand); 'ReLusederes' as 'fletus ederes'; 'omm MMM evolutus' as 'omni re exutus/evolutus'; 'euoroai' as 'enormem'; 'promissaeque barbae impressi artus horrerent' seems corrupt and is rendered tentatively.

Ch. 24: 'aUICUUa' is garbled; read as 'audi' (hear) or similar. Ch. 25: 'Credo, dixit' is awkward; taken as the author imagining what the anger might threaten. Ch. 26: the Scripture cited as 'Exech.' is Ecclus. 34:9; 'Auctoris' is taken as the author of the sin. Ch. 27: 'in pœnitentiam' is taken loosely, with '[but to come]' supplied. 'Felix homo, qui agnoscit ululatum suum' does not match a known biblical verse. Several scripture references in the edition (e.g. Isa. 46, Jer. 14:22) are as printed and appear inexact; Jer. 3:22 is given for the second.

28: 'Dilatio enim tempori confessionem creet' read as 'tempus confessioni'; the following clause ('exaggeratur in dilato damnato … pernaci … cogitat') seems corrupt and is rendered as if 'exaggeratur in dilatione damnatio … pertinaci', with 'cogitat' taken loosely as 'presumes upon'. 'ducetur' read as 'docetur'. 29: 'fillis falce' read as 'finis falce'. 32: 'non peroptatum' is obscure, rendered 'unentreated'; 'dies abcessionis' read as 'abscessionis' (departure).

The closing word 'Victoris' appears to give the author's name as Victor, consistent with the work's pseudo-Ambrosian attribution. The printed page numbers 605 and 606 embedded in the text have been omitted. The Scripture citation corresponds to Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 17:20 in the Vulgate numbering.

nodes.text: ONE BOOK ON PENANCE.

CHAPTER ONE. — As I am about to describe the duties and merits of penance, my dearest brother, I think there is need not of words but of deeds. For a thing wholesome and necessary is not so much to be talked about as taught. Though its whole working is bitter at the root, it bears fruit in an effect of sweetness; it sticks in the throat even as it imparts a saving remedy to the heart. Penance is that in which there is condemnation of the former life and correction promised for the future; and the habit of living is led, as it were, into another life, while the devout mind does not look back at the things that are behind. This I do not so much teach in words as practise in deeds; and although the character of a righteous man does not suit me, yet at the beginning of my discourse I accuse myself. For a careful confession of error has a share of righteousness; because although, as you teach, it belongs to God to punish offences, yet penance practised in humility forestalls the sentence of the judge. For it is written: To the penitent he gave a share of righteousness, and he gathered those who were failing to endure, and appointed them to the lot of truth (Ecclus. 17:20). Come then, penitent, confess your own crimes; lay bare to God the secrets of your iniquity, lay bare the crimes of your heart, and take off the covering of your inner transgression. All the things you have done in secret are known to God: what the tongue has not spoken, the conscience cannot hide. In vain you deceive yourself with a hidden comfort, and think that what you commit without a witness can stay concealed. Everything that is shut is open to God, and whatever the night of hidden thought darkens shines in the open. By the duty of confession make yourself a defendant before yourself; set out your case in your own sight, with yourself as accuser; pronounce sentence against yourself with severity before you feel the anger of the judge; and to draw out mercy, first exercise censure upon yourself. Believe me: everything of which you are suspected becomes at once pardonable when such a penitence of righteousness is found in you, as Scripture says: But to the penitent he gave a share of righteousness, and he gathered those who were failing to endure, and appointed them to the lot of truth. See, the Lord waits for the hands of confession, if guilt does not entangle the one who confesses; and although the conscience of men is known to the divine senses, he has preferred that the tongue should disclose what the hidden places of the heart cannot conceal. Penance, then, is that which doubles different offices in a single act: on the one side it makes the one confessing public, on the other it restores the one who has confessed as innocent; on the one side it puts the guilt up for sale, on the other it excuses the crime; on the one side it sets the sins closer before the sinner, on the other it demands pardon for the penitent. Nor does the Lord allow the one who has confessed to be punished, he who knows how to call back the penitent from condemnation. O magnificent treasure of divine goodness! O singular ordinance of the most merciful judge! He wishes to carve out the voice of confession from the guilty for this purpose: that he may find nothing that must be avenged. And while before the judges of the world the man who has confessed is at once sent to punishment, before the Lord the one who confesses goes straight to pardon; nor does he extract this from the one confessing by other tortures, since the sufferer is seen to carry out the office of terror upon himself. For the groans of the one confessing are gains to the merciful judge, and confession without interrogation is the judge's joy: what is not punished in the servant is gained for the Lord; and much is conferred on the Author if one assigned to punishment comes and is pardoned. For he wishes that to be a loss to vengeance which he does not want to be lost to mercy; nor does he desire to take vengeance, who is ready to have mercy, as he himself says of himself through the prophet: I do not desire the death of the dying so much as that he should turn back and live (Ezek. 18:32). In harmony with this the Wisdom of Solomon says: God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living (Wisd. 1:13). So the mercy of our judge does not wish the guilty to perish to life, but to perish to the sentence; nor does he desire the exile of the dying, but hastens rather to save the one who has confessed: I do not desire, he says, the death of the dying, but that he should turn back and live. Behold the true Author of life, who does not want the death of the dying, but the laments of the converted; and he wants himself always to be beneficent out of compassion, so that justice may not hold the one judged.

CHAPTER II. — He, then, who does not rejoice over one who is lost suffers loss in the one who dies; for in the giver of life a cause of sadness must arise from death — not as though what grieves him in the one lost and dying came down from the law of the bodily senses, since in an incorporeal Author nothing that comes from the body has any force; but because he takes no joy from the death of one who perishes, the act of sadness is ready to hand, so that it is the affection of one who pities, not the anxiety of one who suffers pain, and a sadness flowing from compassion, not from any external passion undergone. It follows, then, that he grieves for the lost who rejoices over the found, and does not rejoice in him dead who is glad of him alive. The Lord shows this through a parable in the Gospel, saying: But you ought to be glad and rejoice, because your brother was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and is found (Luke 15:32). And again: So, he says, there will be joy in heaven before your Father and his angels over one sinner doing penance (ibid. 7). Hence through the prophet Isaiah the Lord calls out the penitent, saying: I am he who blots out your iniquities, and I will not remember them; but you, do not forget, and let us be judged. Tell your iniquities first, that you may be justified (Isa. 43:25–26). What, I ask, is more delightful than this promise? What sweeter can be found than this invitation — to challenge the judge, to speak to him against oneself for oneself, not that he may punish but that he may acquit, not that he may chastise the one who has confessed but that he may justify one convicted by himself? I will not remember, but you, do not forget: that is to say, the memory of your deed will not remain with me if you do not forget your own error; and the disgrace of your crime will be blotted out if, driven by the remembrance of it, you do not cease to confess in my ears. You see, then, that God is intent on the shameful deeds of the sinner if no duty of penance is forthcoming, and that the anger of the just judge hangs over the neck of the guilty man whose confessing groan has not pleased him; but that he leads into forgetfulness the things you have been able to make public, and that the mark of the crime is wiped out if you do not veil your conscience in silence. I am he, he says, who blots out your iniquities, and I will not remember them; but you, do not forget. There ought to be no point of time, no instant of a moment, in which forgetfulness of your sins creeps into your heart; but [remember them] so that you may curse what you committed before, not so that you may be caught by delight in former things; and let there be in you a sigh not from longing for what is past but from the remembrance of sorrow. Keep your fall always before your eyes and mourn it, lament your own death at every moment, feel yourself continually dead, and know without doubt that you are going to die. These things the Lord will not count towards punishment but will turn to glory; and he will so remember you as to forget the things you did before in your sins, and will give you, in return for temporal grief, eternal and infinite comforts, when your sins have escaped unpunished, as he himself says: Blessed are those who mourn now, for they shall be comforted (Matt. 5:5). But you, do not forget, and let us be judged. 'Let us be judged', he says, meanwhile. Will the Lord, then, be judged, he who says that he is to be judged with the sinner? Far from it. Let us be judged, he says: you confessing, I forgiving; you presenting your debts, I by pardoning your sins; you telling your iniquities, I justifying you with complete compassion. Then see what follows: Tell your iniquities first, he says, that you may be justified (Isa. 43:26) — not that you may be condemned; so that there may remain in you the reward of the converted, not the punishment of the confessed; so that the judgement of the just may go with you, not the mark of the damned. And then you will be free of all your iniquities, when you have stood forth as witness and accuser against yourself. Tell your iniquities first, he says, that you may be justified. But does he challenge you to confess your iniquities, brother, as though he were ignorant of them, he who knows them before you commit them? And does he wish to hear from you as though he were unaware, he who is accustomed to judge even those not yet born by his foreknowledge? Or do you not know that in the womb of holy Rebecca the twin offspring, conceived at one time and born at the same, received through the knowledge of foreknowledge a judgement of unequal merits?

CHAPTER III. — So he wishes you rather to know what is going on in you, so that when you disclose your fault to the physician, he may give you the antidote you need to drink; for you will be able to obtain the full benefit of the medicine only if you do not hide the wounds of your conscience from the physician. Otherwise, how will you be cured, when you do not reveal what is hidden in you? For I suppose that unless the physician is called upon, the sick man is not cured. So he waits a long time for the causes of your pain to be shown to him, so that you, once cured, may understand the remedy of the medicine; for you will weigh with just estimation what is owed to the physician if you first acknowledge your illness in yourself. And not to detain you with more words: confession is your medicine, penitent; it cures you, it brings you to life, and it does not allow your wound to keep its rot, but as soon as you have groaned, it draws over it a healing scar. If today some bodily illness afflicts you, and you feel your limbs weighed down by an inward weakness, or you perceive your wound festering with the filth and dirt of rot, you run at once to the physician, you seek a remedy from his art, you keep watch before the door of the sleeping man, and you stand before his doors as an early-morning caller; you pray with entreaties, promise gifts, offer presents, and are eager to hand over your whole inheritance for your health. And although very often through his lack of skill the illness either grows worse or is at least drawn out over a long time, you nevertheless persevere in constant attendance; you, a man, hope from a man for slow remedies, and do not despair of help that will be of use, though you do not yet feel the effect of strengthening. And yet you do not run to your God, the physician who costs nothing, the willing apothecary, who in curing the illnesses of your soul knows no weariness, nor looks for a fee from your health, but rather wishes to reward with a fee the one he has cured. And indeed the temporal physician cures only what concerns the body, but God heals the soul, which sins have wounded all over; the one offers remedies that help for the present, but the other applies a lasting medicine. And yet a man who is a physician cannot even help himself unless God comes to his aid; for the cleverness of medicine very often labours in vain if God does not wish to prolong the sick man's time of life. We shall sometimes see that they cannot help even themselves, when, overtaken by bodily ailments, they are cheated of the benefit of health. There will be no benefit, then, from medicine when medicine does not help the physician himself. No one, believe me, restores you better than he who made you; nor does anyone else justify except he who scourges and cures. He alone knows how to mend the breakages of his own work, and to reshape the shattered form of our clay into the substance of its original state, as he himself says through the prophet: As the potter's clay, he says, so are you in my hand (Jer. 18:6). Nor does he do this after any interval of time: as soon as you have told your fault, he at once grants help as well. Between imploring aid and receiving remedies almost no time comes between: he waits only for this, that you confess; there will be no delay in your being healed. Tell your iniquities first, he says, that you may be justified. The same Spirit promises this to the unjust through the prophet Ezekiel: The wicked man, on whatever day he turns from injustice and does justice, on that very day all his injustices will perish; in his injustice which he did he will not die (Ezek. 18:27). And elsewhere: When you have turned and groaned, then you will be saved (Isa. 30:15).

CHAPTER IV. — But perhaps you will say: I have no accomplice-witness, and the things I have committed are known to no one at all. What then, if you have no witness? Do you at least not know that God, who knows beforehand, is the inescapable witness of your conscience? And if no human being knows your deeds, surely God knows your deeds beforehand, and even those still to come. For what does he not see, who sees everywhere and sees the whole, as he himself says to Job: Who would think that anything is hidden from me? Give me a place where God is not, from whom [nothing] is hidden at all, and you too will be hidden in your deeds, as you suppose. But God is everywhere, and is whole in the whole, as he himself says: Heaven is my seat, and the earth the footstool of my feet (Isa. 66:1); and: I fill heaven and earth (Jer. 23:24). Hence also the most blessed prophet David says: Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your face? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend to the underworld, you will come there. If I take up my wings straight, to dwell in the farthest part of the sea, even there your hand, Lord, will lead me, and your right hand will hold me (Ps. 138[139]:7 ff.). In vain, then, do you say that you have no witness, when you hear that God is whole everywhere and spread through all things by the compass of his majesty, so that whatever is thought hidden is known to him. But, you will say, I have no witness. You would have said this rightly if you did not have the example of Cain, the first of parricides. Parricidal impiety had persuaded his devout brother to go with him into the field, and a brotherhood still raw and new, thinking it need not guard itself against a brother, headlong obeyed him out of the goodness of simplicity. The two brothers walk together in one company, and the ill-starred parricide chose, as he thought, a place without a witness to carry out the plan of his wicked crime. As if, indeed, because he had no human witness, anything could have escaped the eyes of God; or as if he could conceal anything by seeking solitude, when nothing is concealed from the gaze of the Author. But when the first contriver of an unspeakable deed judged the place fit for committing the outrage, he leapt into fury and, at the devil's instigation, killed his most patient brother, who offered no resistance at all. The fact was indeed evident in its result, but, as far as Cain had reckoned, having been committed without a witness, it lay hidden. And the cruellest of men believed that he need not confess a crime committed without a witness, though he acknowledged the crime by the very fact that he wished to hide it. But behold the Lord of things, to whom whatever is thought hidden is in plain view, and from whom what is done in the secret places of thought cannot be hidden, as Scripture says: The thought of man will confess to you (Ps. 75[76]:11); and again: Your eyes saw my imperfect [being], and in your book all will be written (Ps. 138[139]:16); and again: God who searches hearts and reins (Ps. 7:10). Hence the same prophet David says: You saw my thoughts from afar (Ps. 138[139]:2). [The Lord] calls the parricide with the voice of one indignant. And knowing that the savage spirit which he had shown in the fierce deed would deny it, in order to heap up the guilt of the impious parricide, he pretends not to know, as it were, what had been committed. And the Lord, it says, said to Cain: Where is Abel your brother? And Cain said: I do not know; am I my brother's keeper? (Gen. 4:9). O detestable madness! O unparalleled audacity! Confidently he denies what he had committed without a witness, and believed that the crime could not be made public without a witness, when by the very affair he was rather betraying the guilt of his conscience. What are you doing, unhappy Cain? You have no human witness: see, you have the shed blood as your betrayer; it itself makes you known and accuses you. Its voice appeals to the Author against you, and the spilt gore stirs up odium, so that vengeance may not pass over the hidden parricide. What, he says, have you done? See, the voice of your brother's blood cries to me from the earth (ibid., 10). But when the parricide perceived that what he thought hidden was betrayed, and, convicted by the blood as witness, that he had feigned obstinate denials in vain, he confesses the deed: he longs for a harsher judgement to be pronounced against himself, since his conscience could not excuse the parricide he had committed. But the more severe penalty is deferred for a time, so that a slow sentence might butcher the author of so great a crime for longer, and the swiftness of the punishment imposed might not seem rather a shortcut for the condemned; and so that the crime of parricide might be drawn out long by penal duration, which [a swift] death [as for] brigandage would have lessened. Why then do you flatter yourself on the ground that you have no witness, when you see that Cain was both convicted by the testimony of innocent blood and punished?

CHAPTER V. — But, you will say, I have no witness to spread abroad my deeds. I ask you, tell me: if you have no witness, do you not have the testimony of conscience? Or can you escape yourself and avoid your conscience? Conscience, I say, with which nothing that we do dies, which accuses and judges us in our deeds; which, though it has no use of speech, yet does not know how to keep silent. A witness can be removed by death; the absence of a witness can help you for a time: this is always with you, and does not exist without you; it clings to your breast and never deserts you; and like some attendant it departs from you at no interval of time: it holds you guilty and always captive under its own authority. If ever a happier course of prosperous affairs has distracted your mind, and your senses have begun to take pleasure in delight over what was done, suddenly it goads you, it strikes you to the marrow and breaks in upon your senses, interrupts your joy, and troubles the whole region of your breast with sorrowful sighs; and as though it were held wounded by disgrace, no remedy is found for a man by which it may be cured; for it is always offended when another is chastised, and in another's wound it is itself struck first. Next, do you want to know how great is the severity of conscience? A witness can be corrupted for you with gold, can be bought with money: conscience admits no corruption; its testimony remains whole, fortified with the full firmness of faithfulness. Moreover, against a witness an advocate is hired, and by the ingenuity of the defence arguments of cunning are sought out, and the truth of testimony is perverted by the craft of shameless speech; the judge too is bought off, so that the nature of the deed may be excused. All these things are void where conscience is present; and though a man dies, conscience surely does not die, which after the death of the body is judged in the soul. And do you think it helps you that you have no witness, when you feel the daily and perpetual judgement of conscience? But clearly divine vengeance will not attend the one whom his own conscience has judged; for the power of the judge must be idle there, where the guilty man, aware of himself, has stood forth as witness and accuser against himself. For without doubt the case of sin will be doubled if an obstinate conscience refuses to confess its deeds; for then one who has been hardened in confessing his sins becomes impious instead of a sinner, so that a fitting sentence may both bind his outrages and the stubborn conscience may pay the penalty of obstinacy. For the agitation of the judge is broken when the strenuous strictness of severity is softened by the assault of penitence and confession: a judgement brought forth in indignation is struck down by satisfaction, and the purpose of the one threatening is tempered by the modesty of most humble prayer. Learn this from the Ninevites, by whose confession a sentence already pronounced was blotted out and impending wrath turned aside, so that confessing penance should not be in vain. A sentence already hurled from heaven hung over the wretched city, and the axe of divine punishment pressed upon the necks of the unhappy. The heavenly sword had already been drawn from its sheath, and vehement wrath was blazing to avenge the crimes committed. The voice of the herald threatened the peoples with destruction, and the prophet's cry announced to all who were to perish an imminent end: In three days, he says, the city of Nineveh too will be overthrown. Alas, why, crimes, do you exact it from God; why, sins, do you buy it? You have forestalled the most merciful compassion of our God, from whom you have exacted a vengeance so near and before its time. And so I seem to myself to see what great distress hemmed in the wretched, and what necessity had gripped them in trembling. Fear had lost counsel, despair had no remedy; for the swiftness of the time was so headlong that not even the span allotted relieved the dreadful apprehension of the crime. In three days, he says, Nineveh will be overthrown (Jonah 3:4). And what sort of overthrow was that to be which is proclaimed to those who were to perish? It certainly did not signify a hostile incursion, nor the din of arms nor the terrible blare of trumpets, against which perhaps the defences of those resisting could have stood, or a contest between the sides could have been joined in declared battle, or by the safety of flight they could have cast off the lot of captives; but a destruction of divine indignation and heavenly vengeance is proclaimed, in which the one to be punished is neither withdrawn by flight nor given the means of defending himself by the arts of war. For who could avoid an imposed destruction which a crash from the sky was beginning to pour out?

CHAPTER VI. — But see, counsel does not desert the wretched in their fear, and despair finds a remedy out of the danger. Returning to themselves, they question their consciences in the place of a judge; they run to the bulwark of penance and, setting up the shield of confession, turn aside the arrow. All go to the cure of confessing their crimes, and the crowd exposed to death joins together in the duty of satisfaction. Those about to perish proclaim for themselves a necessary fast; in their very bodies they chastise their souls with the scourge of humility: they put on sackcloth instead of clothing, and instead of ointments they sprinkle themselves with ash, and lying prostrate on the ground they lick the dust. They mourn their own death with tears as at a funeral, and accompany their life with laments; they make their guilt public with groans, and lay open the secret misdeeds of their actions. Every age and sex without distinction fits itself to the offices of mourning: all finery laid aside, ornaments thrown down; but clearly that squalor of the body was the adornment of penance, and the strength of their condition was the highest glory of confession. Nourishment was denied even to infants at the breast, and an age not yet stained with its own sins bore the burdens of others. Dumb cattle went hungry for their food, and the brute animal did not receive its natural fodder. A single wailing of differing natures was heard throughout the walls of the city, and through all the houses of the town the tearful laments of the mourners resounded; and, to put it in a word, the earth bore the lowing of those confessing, and the very stars echoed with the voice of penance. What is written was fulfilled: The prayer of one who humbles himself has pierced the clouds (Sir. 35:21). So, in the end, it appeased the offended God, so it made the stern one mild, so it soothed the angry one, and put the sword-point of vengeance back in its sheath; because conscience passed judgement on itself. Confession snatched the guilty from punishment, and penance claimed for itself those already handed over to vengeance. The record of condemnation was at once blotted out by the tears of those confessing, and the affirmation confessing the crime absolved those liable to punishment. The merciful God saw that the penitent had brought judgement upon themselves and were condemning the errors of their conscience by that affirmation; immediately he granted pardon to those he had destined for punishment, and at once spared the afflicted, so that, exempted from torment, they might become the gain of compassion. The testimony of prophecy which we set out a little earlier above was proved: I am he who blots out your iniquities, and I will not remember them; but you, do not forget, and let us be judged [together] (Isa. 43:25–26). Tell your iniquities first, he says, that you may be justified; and again: When you have turned and groaned, then you will be saved (Isa. 30:15); and again: Turn to the Lord your God, for he is merciful and compassionate, patient and of great mercy, and one who bends his sentences against the wickednesses committed (Joel 2:13). Hence also the most blessed David says: I have known my sin, and I have not covered my iniquity. I said, I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the iniquity of my sin (Ps. 31[32]:5); and again: For I know my iniquity, and my sin is always before me (Ps. 50[51]:5). You see, then, that one who sins daily needs judgement upon himself, by which, when conscience is laid bare, it is covered; and when it is made public, it is covered. And although everything we do is known to God, and is not hidden from his senses before it happens, he nevertheless prefers you to lay bare the secret of your heart and disclose the misdeeds of your conscience, so that by the gift of his indulgence he may cover the nakedness of your shame. How much he wishes to release the one confessing with pardon! Of such, stripped [of their sins], the most blessed Prophet sang, saying: Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered (Ps. 31[32]:1). Although this more evidently belongs to the reborn, whose iniquities and crimes are covered and hidden in baptism; for a confession that is not faithless holds a sure place of pardon, and a penitent conscience is safe if it does not doubt the remission of indulgence.

CHAPTER VII. But on the contrary the heap of sin is raised higher if what is committed is denied. We mentioned this above in the deed of Cain: while he thought to deny his crime to his Author, he was not permitted to exempt himself from punishment, so that his conscience, in the atrocity of his deed, deprived him through his denial of the public fruit of penance. For he was convicted while denying, not confessing of his own will, and his obstinacy was punished [...], because confessing penance did not follow the question put to him. It is right, then, to lay open here step by step the sevenfold reason for that vengeance, and to show by proof of the evident facts what causes compelled so harsh a sentence to be heaped up, so that the enormity of the vengeance may not lie open to suspicion of injustice or false accusation. Yet a vehement punishment ought to accompany the invention of a new crime, so that it might serve as an example to later generations. For he errs who thinks the parricide was held guilty of only one crime, since all crimes are crowded together in the testimony of such a wickedness. For hear that the Lord said: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your strength, and you shall love your neighbour as yourself (Matt. 22:37ff.); whence on these two commandments hang the whole Law and the prophets. Since, then, all that belongs to the Law hangs on these two precepts, and I see that Cain neither loved God, whose first workmanship he violated, and that he vehemently hated his brother, whom he killed at the prompting of impiety, it is plain that he has paid until now the debt of vengeance, since in his deed all crimes are found to meet. And rightly a sevenfold punishment was exacted from him, in whom crimes of every kind held the first place. And yet I detect in him specifically seven outrages, to each of which its own torment is assigned. For the first crime is that he did not divide rightly; that is, he ate first of the first fruits of the earth before he offered them. The second is that, when he appeared to have received a deserved rejection of his gift, he conceived a defiant spirit; and though his pious brother bore no blame for the rejected offering, the ill-starred man believed that he would avenge himself on the Author if for this he killed the brother whom God plainly approved. The third crime is that, filled with the gall of envy and poisoned with the bitterness of spite, he was jealous with savage animosity of his most innocent brother. The fourth is that he deceived by guile the brother who complied with him, so that they went together into the field, where the just man was to begin martyrdom in the simplicity of a sheep, and the unjust man to stain the earth with parricide. The fifth is that the wicked author of cruelty killed his brother. The sixth, that when he had committed the crime he also denied it, and thought God ignorant of any deed, though he had perceived that God had punished the secret of his conscience when he received a fitting rejection in the refusal of his offering. The seventh crime is that he did not believe that, once exposed, he would be punished after death for the parricide, since because of the infamy of the crime made public he asked to be killed in the present time. Rightly, then, was vengeance taken on Cain sevenfold, on whom as many torments were bestowed as there were crimes. On him were inflicted as many blows as causes are counted, so that justice did not exceed the measure of vengeance, nor did fitting vengeance fall short of the number of crimes. I have set this down again for this reason, that the occasion for the exposition I had introduced might not pass by.

CHAPTER VIII. I feel that I have long strayed from the purpose of the work I began, and turned aside into another line of discourse. But the return to the rest of the course left off is easy, and the path of the subject turned from is quickly regained, when the argument does not wander outside the bounds of the proof inserted into it. So, he says, I knew my sin, and did not cover my iniquity. I said, I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the iniquity of my sin (Ps. 31[32]:5); and again: For I know my iniquity, and my sin is always before me (Ps. 50[51]:5). This he not only taught in words but fulfilled in deeds; for it is not enough for the perfection of spiritual wisdom to display virtue in words unless the teaching is adorned by deeds. Only then is fitting authority granted to teaching, if it rests on its own example. Accordingly the Lord says in the Gospel: Whoever does and so teaches will be called greatest in the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 5:19); so that teaching may be strengthened by deed, and the credibility of deeds may receive testimony from teaching. Otherwise the teaching that abuses the glory of eloquence with the trappings of words will not be founded on firm strength; for the tongue will be rich, but the conscience will not be full of the riches of works, and he who enjoys another's privilege will be deprived of his own merit. Let us see, then, what he did who sang these things. At one time two sins had crept upon the king, and the licence of kingship had enticed the prince into committing a crime; for while he wished to cover adultery, he fell into the crime of homicide. Yet he did neither through the violence of royal descent nor through ambition for power; for although the adultery came from the licence of unchastity, the homicide had not been committed out of hatred. So a prophet is sent by the Lord to plead before him the case of the adultery and the slaughter of the slain man, and under the colour of a made-up tale to draw a judgement from him unawares. But when the prophet had set out what he had proposed, the king, moved, passes in truth a sentence against himself that he had not meant for himself, and as an unknowing arbiter brings vengeance upon himself. Then, when the judge, caught beforehand, saw himself struck by his own judgement, and as a most just examiner found himself guilty, and felt that he could not escape the penalty of a judgement in which the judge himself was held in the condition of the condemned, he seized the most salutary counsel in such straits: since he could not appeal against the justice of the judgement, he took refuge in the inner chamber of penance. He knew that his sin was exposed, and he veiled his iniquity with no cloud of denial: he at once spoke testimony against himself, and, having uttered the voice of confession, immediately obtained pardon of his sins. For he says: I have sinned against the Lord. And the prophet interposed no delays of absolution and did not postpone the effect of forgiveness: as soon as the exposed culprit made confession, he brought forth to him by the will of God the pardon of his crimes, saying: The Lord has taken away your sin (2 Sam. 12:13). So was fulfilled what he sang in the psalm, saying: I knew my sin, and did not cover my iniquity. I said, I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the iniquity of my sin (Ps. 31[32]:5).

CHAPTER IX. Let us also lay open another example of penance in holy David. For this outstanding king, by the pattern of a life worth imitating, had bound himself to divine worship in faithful service, so as to leave us not merely examples of his ways but monuments of them. Against a prohibition he had ordered the people to be counted, and had wished to know the size of the whole army. The royal will was obeyed, and the numbered total of the whole host was reported, and the illustrious man began to know what did him harm: he exalted his good fortune in the increase of his people, and counted the gains of a multiplied army among princely joys. Soon another prophet is sent to him, and the cause of his sin is not set before him subtly, as was done the first time: now a choice of penalties is put to him for the deed. And the word of the Lord came to Gad the prophet, saying: Go to David and say: Thus says the Lord: I lay three things upon you; choose for yourself one of them, and I will do it to you. And Gad came to David and told him, saying: Choose for yourself which of the three you wish to be done: either famine for three years over the land, or for three months to flee before your enemies while they pursue you, or for three days death in the land; and now know and see what I shall answer to him who sent the word to you (2 Sam. 24:11ff.). What struggle of counsel, then, turned in his mind? What turmoil of thought in the choice! On one side fear of enemies, on another the devastation of famine, on another the stroke of divine punishment terrified him. He would have wished none of these to befall, but the offence could not remain unpunished. In the very straits of the choice, hemmed in by the crisis of danger on either hand, taught by the example of his earlier pardon, he chooses in that very turmoil the harsher punishment, and gave himself up to the greater penalty so that he might call forth clemency. For the rigour of justice is softened when mercy is relied upon, and before the most clement judge the cause of mercy is heard first; for he who forgives errors to those who confess does not condemn by his will, but condemns the obstinate. And so this devout king, in the storm of deliberation, did not let go the anchor of penance; and, trusting in the mercy of the one who terrified him, he did not consider the magnitude of the vengeance. And David, it says, said to Gad: I am in great distress over these three, but it is better for me to fall into the hands of the Lord, for his mercy is very great, than to fall into the hands of men. Vengeance follows at once on his consent, and an appeasable penalty accompanies an appeasing choice: an innumerable slaughter of the dead takes place, and a multitude of the people is slain by the angel's stroke. Seventy thousand of the army are struck down, and the pitiable ruin of the camp pressed more bitterly on his gentle spirit. As author of the deed he sets himself before the weapon of punishment, and against the raging sword of justice he puts on the breastplate of confession; insisting rather that he himself be punished among the punished, he cries out and wishes the sentence to be turned upon himself, so that he might call back the blow from the people. See, it is I, he says, I the shepherd have sinned, and I have done evil; but this flock, what has it done? Turn your hand against me and against my father's house (2 Sam. 24:17). See, by the duty of satisfaction the penalty is struck down, and by the arms of confession indignation is fought off, so that vengeance went no further against him, and the shaking poured from heaven upon the people ceased. By one act of penance he both purchased mercy for himself and at once halted vengeance from the people, so that, pardoned by merit, he might sing, saying: I said, I will confess my iniquity against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the impiety of my sin (Ps. 31[32]:5); for when he stood in the despair of one convicted, he deserved to be reckoned worthy of expiation. But, [you say,] the enormity of your sins presses on you, and, a captive under their dominion, you do not dare to raise your eyes to heaven. I approve, indeed, the fear of conscience; I do not praise the counsel. I would rather you were uncertain about obtaining indulgence than utterly despairing of the restoration of salvation.

CHAPTER X. — For the confusion of the one who supplicates holds a certain part of confession: aware of its own sins, it does not doubt the forgiveness of the Author, but blushes at the greatness of its own crime. For to have acknowledged guilt is the beginning of confession, and what remorse spurs on becomes nearest to pardon. But, you will say, the abundance of my sins drives me back. On the contrary, you must press on with the duty of confession all the more, the more you are loaded with the burdens of sins, so that what you are not worthy to demand through friendship you may be able to obtain through shamelessness. For you hear in the Gospel that the Lord said that the one to whom little is forgiven loves less (Luke 7:47). Further, you make God impious if you think that he rejects the one who has turned back, and denies affection to one returning, when you know that by him the lost are sought out with the affection of compassion. The Apostle proves this, saying: And if we have been unfaithful, he himself will remain faithful; he cannot deny himself (2 Tim. 2:13). Or do you not know that the Lord, tempted nine times in the desert, put off vengeance, and that not even at the tenth time of tempting could he have condemned their hardness, if after the nine past faults the people had done penance, as he himself says: See, already ten times they have provoked me in this desert (Num. 14:22)? Read the book of Judges, and you will find that on countless occasions the children of Israel did evil before the Lord and were handed over to the incursions of the nations; but that again the people, having turned back, were freed from various captivities through chosen leaders, and that what they committed could not have been punished if fitting penance had followed each time the deed was done; for although penal correction was not lacking, yet it was not a cutting-off unto perdition, but a plea for conversion. For when a chastised son is received back into affection, it is clear that he has been admonished to the duty of satisfaction, not punished; nor does the correction seem to be of hatred but of love, since the rights of fatherly love are not denied to one who returns again and again after the scourge. Finally, hear the Lord through the prophet, rebuking with such a lash the harlot, given over to shameful deeds and defiled with contagions, and yet willing to take her back to himself by right of conversion: And I said, he says, after you had committed fornication in all these things, return to me; and faithless Judah did not return (Jer. 3:7). The same the Lord makes plain in the Gospel when he rebukes the hardened, saying: Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you, how often I wished to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not (Matt. 23:37)! Believe me, the Lord awaits the last act of our life, and in whatever state the final end finds us, in that he will judge us; so that, even if, hedged about with manifold errors, the shadows of misdeeds swirl above your head, the darkness of crimes clouds your eyes, the yoke of sin bends your neck, and within the inner chamber of your conscience the shame of outrages repeatedly makes the wound fester, if you do not cast your soul down into the abjection of despair, when you have poured out in confession a single word from the secret around your heart, he will not deny the remedy of pardon who came to save souls, not to destroy them; for since he does not desire the death of the dying, he without doubt urges the one who has turned back towards life, as the Lord himself says: The Son of Man did not come to destroy the souls of men, but to save [them] (Luke 9:56); and again: For the Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost (Luke 19:10). Unless indeed you make the devil all-powerful, if you think that the Lord cannot snatch the captive from his jaws; or that, just as he is always watchful to destroy, the Lord is not as busy to win.

CHAPTER XI. — In this, then, let the last-moment confession of the thief lead you, as with confidence drawn from a present instance, and let the final confession on the cross of one who did not despair give the greatest hope to the despairing. That man had stained the whole course of his life with bloody robberies, and had always acted in the world as an armour-bearer of diabolical savagery; he had never remembered God, had heard none of the commandments of the Law, or certainly, if he had heard them, being more inclined to crimes, he paid them no heed; he turned all his hope into despair, and practised cruelty in the manner of criminal henchmen. For this he was condemned on the cross, and hung fastened to the wood together with his very crimes. At last the lost man came to his senses, and, placed in the very punishment, he purchased for himself a great gain from death; for he recognised the God with whom he hung; he trembled before the future judge to whom he clung; he made public the crimes of his conscience; at once he gained the baptism of the outpouring of blood; and he entered paradise with the Lord, a confessor clad in purple. This is the true counsel of penance, this the chief rule of confessing: that you believe the Son of God, whom you know to be the Author, also to be the Judge, as he himself says: The Father judges no one, but has given all judgement to the Son (John 5:22); and that, to lay hold of the hope of eternal salvation, you do not take thought for the present life but reflect on the future judgement. For first the condemned man exposed himself in the sight of the judge, and, confessing his crimes, fulfilled the duty of a penitent; then, when he saw the punishment of the cross, he understood that the sentence was shared by the one fastened [beside him], not the cause; yet he believed in God at the very time when Judaea stubbornly denied him; and, not forgetful of the future judgement while on the cross, he commended the memory of himself to the judgement of the one who was to reign. The Gospel makes this plain: But the other thief, it says, answering, rebuked him, saying: Do you not fear God, you who are under the same condemnation? We indeed justly receive as we have done; but this man has committed no evil. And he said to Jesus: Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom (Luke 23:40–42). But see at once what he earned, what he heard from the mouth of Truth, what he received from the grace of the judge: Amen I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43).

CHAPTER XII. — But you tell me: I have added sins to sins, and I who, already falling, had been raised up, have fallen again, and the wound of my conscience, already almost healed, has broken open afresh with the festering of sin. Why do you tremble? What do you fear? He who healed you before is always the same; you will not change physician. He will not labour to examine the cause of your illness, nor will he attempt to test anew on you the power of a medicine; he will heal you with a familiar antidote. He who knows the origin of your sickness does not await a trial of the remedy. By that by which you were cured before, you will be cured again: neither will you be doubtful of the healing remedy, nor the physician uncertain of your restoration. He will certainly chastise your intemperance, and lash your impatience with harsh rebuke; but he who does not despise the sick will not deny help. Hear the Prophet saying: Will not he who sleeps rise again? (Ps. 40[41]:9). Or does not one who has been shipwrecked sail again in the same way? Or one who has lost a harvest, once he has despaired, does he not plough or sow again? This course of ours is tossed on a kind of sea of the world: we must sail, and spread our sails against the snares of evils. The gale rages, the wind rises, the storm runs mad: if you so hold the helm that you do not lose the moorings of your ship, you will make for port with your cargo unharmed; but if, dashed by hostile waves on entangling rocks and hindered by blasts, you are shipwrecked amid the warring straits of the swelling flood, you must go back to the ballast, first refit the vessel, buy goods, undergo dangers again, and work out the causes of the past disaster; and in order to recover what was lost, you will not hesitate to commit yourself to the old peril under an uncertain hope. For without doubt you will become a beggar if after the shipwreck you refuse to return to the practice of trading; nor will you be able afterwards to complain of your want and hardships, if, overtaken by the lot of shipwreck, you are made through the torpor of idleness a beggar by calamity. And if this is the care of a worldly merchant, that often after the loss of shipwreck he does not despair that his past losses may be made good by the profit of industry, nor, stripped by attacks, does he allow his nakedness to be exposed, but rather strives to grow from little, and with doubtful hopes hunts to gain greater profits, with sin acting as go-between; how much more must you consider the losses of your soul, and at once repair the loss in which the losses of future hope are counted and the gain of eternal life is unhappily lost!

CHAPTER XIII. — You must go to the treasury of a fitting giver; and, with interest of penance and satisfaction offered as payment, draw up bonds, send signed notes, buy from him gold refined in fire by the gift of God, fill your vessel with goods of whatever kind, if not precious ones, spend your wealth in purchasing that precious pearl with which you may adorn the ugliness of your soul; so that when you come to the great city with your goods brought in, you may be richer in worthier profits and most blessed wares. For if the torpor of sloth seizes you, and the idleness of the body begins to rule the senses, and you seek no means of restoring your soul, you will be subjected to the tortures of the creditor and held liable for the interest. That liberal sentence will be pronounced which, aware of yourself, you will not be able to escape, or suspend by interposing the voice of appeal: To everyone who has it will be given, and he will abound; but from him who has not, even what he has will be taken from him (Matt. 25:29); and: Cast the useless servant out into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matt. 25:30). You do not bear to put on your tunic made from wool-work of the cheapest kind; you shudder at your garment, should it be disfigured by a stain; and you do not shudder at your soul, which is polluted by the filth of sin and the defilement of crime! Indeed, you hasten at that same moment to wash the tunic, so that you can put it on clean and without any blemish of foulness; but you do not long to recover for your soul the whiteness stained by the squalor of crimes, nor do you desire your conscience to be washed, which you know to be muddy with the filth of outrages and the contamination of crimes. Who, I ask, falls and does not seek to rise? Who is sick and does not long to recover? Who is in danger and does not wish to escape? Who, made poor, does not desire to restore his patrimony? If the nature of things allowed that, when such misfortunes arise, someone could not return to the quality of his former state, [then] imitate your former ways, so as to receive worse; let your hands fall, and wrap your half-waking eyes in dullness, fall asleep never to wake, lie never to rise, and crush your dull mind with the stupor of sleep. You will repent afterwards of your slowness, when you have taken thought for nothing that profits the welfare of your soul. You will always be lying sick, helpless, worn out by poverty, and, so to speak, drunk with the intoxication of sleep, about to hear that verdict which you will never be free of: They have slept their sleep, and found nothing (Ps. 75[76]:6). Arise, brother, arise, and drive off the torpor of unsound counsel; keep watch, always keep watch, and be anxious for your salvation, not so as to sleep in despair. Beware the thief by night, lest he dig through the wall of your house, and avoid the noonday archer of the flying arrow; for careless security lies open to attacks, and one who sleeps is easily crept up on so as to be struck fatally. In the watchful there is confidence, in the sleeper nothing is safe: it befits a sober mind to have sleep as a servant, not a master. The enemy flees whom he does not find asleep: And blessed will be the servant whom his master on coming finds watching (Matt. 24:46); for he says: Rise, you who sleep, arise from the dead (Eph. 5:14), and lay hold of Christ.

CHAPTER XIV. — But I do not dare, you will say, to pray, because my conscience holds me back; for I have erred not once, but more often and repeatedly. But I will say: If shame holds you back from praying, let your stubbornness in sinning cease, and what you fear will become a benefit of fear, not a cause of despair. For to stand in awe of the judge's power will be a matter not of disgrace but of modesty; for although the licence of sinning may be frequent, yet the conscience becomes excusable which timidity has borne in the remembrance of sin. Let the example of Ahab, that most impious king, teach you. For he had coveted the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite, because it bordered on his own property. He offers a price, or at least a vineyard of equal size in exchange; the other refused, declaring that he could by no means transfer to another a thing that was his inheritance. Stung by this refusal, he returns home sad, because the desire of his appetite had come to nothing. Then his sacrilegious wife Jezebel asks the causes of her husband's sadness; and having learned them, she applied, as it were, the tinder of consolation to his wounded heart: by this art, with many slanders contrived by falsehood through the counsel of the impure woman, the innocent Naboth is stoned to death. Having fulfilled the outrage of her deadly wish, the woman goes in to her husband as a victor, to tell him the joy of the slain man's death; and so as not to be held alone in the crime, she acted with the cunning of the first woman, to bind her husband to complicity in the wickedness, and to tie both spouses, as accomplices, with one chain of crime. Rise, she says, take possession of the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite, who would not give it to you for a price; for see, he is dead (3 Kgs 21:15). But he, grieving that he had furnished the occasion of the slain man's death, shudders at the news of the crime, and bewails the cause of his death with tearful grief; for, having torn his royal garments, he girds himself in mourning dress, bearing witness not so much to the guilt of complicity as to repentance for his first thought. And it came to pass, it says, when Ahab heard that Naboth the Jezreelite was dead, he tore his garments, and girded himself with sackcloth (ibid., 16). Ahab, then, could have been free of the guilt of the blood that was shed, because he had done penance for his design, not for the murder, and the impiety of the homicide had remained with the profane woman, who thought she ought to buy the vineyard at the price, as it were, of blood shed. But see, like a dog returned to his vomit, he becomes hateful: forgetting his repentance, Ahab at once lays aside his mourning and goes to take possession of the slain man's vineyard. And he loses the merit of innocence who, lured by desire for the vineyard, joined his consent to the killing of the murdered man. Soon the venerable prophet Elijah is sent to him as messenger, and sentence is pronounced against him with indignation, so that the penance done earlier was made void, and the doubled presumption of the crime gave occasion for vengeance. And Elijah said to Ahab: Thus says the Lord: See, I am bringing evils upon you, and I will cut [them] off after you, and I will destroy from Ahab him that pisses against the wall, and him that is shut up and left in Israel; and I will make the house of Ahab like the house of Jeroboam son of Nebat, and like the house of Baasha son of Ahijah, for all the things by which you have provoked God, and have made Israel turn aside (ibid., 21 ff.). But he, since he could not escape the blow of the sentence, suddenly returns to his former counsel of penance, confesses his guilt with weeping, cast down his royal power with sackcloth, put on the sack of penance, and, standing in awe of the face of the one who threatened, by silent groaning he made his offence public, and did not excuse his conscience. It came to pass, it says, when Ahab heard these words, he stood in awe before the face of the Lord, and went about weeping, and tore his garments, and girded himself with sackcloth. Then the Lord said to Elijah: Have you seen how Ahab has stood in awe before my face? I will not bring evils in his days, but in the days of his son I will bring [them] (ibid., 27 ff.). See to what point fearful reverence led, and how great a weight of severity fear broke! It was not the pomp of prayer, not ornament of speech, nor abundance of eloquence that pleased God, but many prayers of tears. The mouth was silent, but the heart groaned; he wept with his eyes, but his conscience wailed, and the mercy of the Author praised the reverence of his repentance. It would have been little for the guilty man to have escaped the punishment due, had his reverence not received the testimony of approval. And he was approved in fear who was being condemned in crime; nor was his earlier mourning for the slain man's death in vain; but the fault repeated again and again he purged by renewed lamentation.

CHAPTER XV. — Nor should King Manasseh, son of Hezekiah, be passed over in silence, who, outstripping the audacity of all the profane, stretched out impious hands against God, and, degenerating from his father's ways, raised his insane head altogether for the worship of idols instead of divine worship. For, possessed by sacrilegious fury, he set up altars in the house of God to an accursed superstition, defiled it with images of demons, filled the holy altars of the temple with stone figures, tended groves, dedicated his sons to profane fire, sought auguries, polluted his life with sorceries, led the people into the observances of idols, defiled [them] with ceremonies, sold [them] into bondage to the devil, and practised, beyond all the insolence of a desperate mind, everything that is forbidden by the divine laws. For these so many and so great outrages he was carried off as plunder, and bound with iron chains and weighed down with fetters, he endured the punishment of a captive, and, transported to Babylon, he paid the penalty of his impiety; so that, delivered over, he felt the divine vengeance which, hardened, he had never before remembered. At length, chastised by a fitting scourge, he is converted, and, placed in punishment, he acknowledged God, whom, set in his kingdom, he had not sought before. Affliction profited the desperate man, and his wickedness was corrected into acknowledgement by the goad of correction. That vengeance was a medicine for a lost mind, and the chastisement contributed much to his salvation, which struck the impious man for this reason, to make acceptable to God the one whom the devil had made a stranger through lack of self-control; and what had been inflicted on his vanity profited the health of his soul. The faith of the Lord's scripture confirms this: And the Lord spoke, it says, against Manasseh and against the people, and they did not listen; and the Lord brought upon them the commanders of the armies of the Assyrians, and they seized Manasseh, and bound him with chains and fetters, and led him to Babylon. And soon, being afflicted, he sought the Lord his God, and humbled himself greatly before the face of the God of his fathers, and prayed to God, and the Lord heard him, and brought him back to Jerusalem, into his kingdom. And Manasseh knew that the Lord himself is God. See how much of sudden lamentation from a converted heart washed away and cleansed his sin, and wiped away with tears what wickedness had stained. Yet he prayed conscious of his guilt; and he earned the right to purchase pardon by satisfaction, so much so that he restored to their former veneration those holy things which he had once defiled by the contamination of profane acts, and returned everything to the worship of the fear of God. In the completion of the convert's turning was fulfilled that prophetic oracle of the divine mouth: When you have turned and groaned, then you will be saved (Isa. 30:15).

CHAPTER XVI. — But why should I make mention of those kings whom the praiseworthy origin of a chosen race did not allow to depart, by the worst persuasion, from the city of sacred religion, when that savage Nebuchadnezzar, a foreign prince, was punished by divine chastisement, so that through the correction of vengeance he was compelled to acknowledge the one whom he had dared to deny by sacrileges, and to believe through mighty works in the one whom through ferocity of spirit he had not known before: so much so that he who, lifted up by a stubborn spirit, had not before feared to be proclaimed a god, afterwards did not dare to speak falsely about His incomparable majesty; since, corrected by the great wonder of what had been done to him, he did not cease to confess the one true God with his whole heart and by proclaiming decrees? But if, conscious of evil, you are in awe of praying, you have the teaching of the publican; even if you harbour the suspicion that when you pray for your sins you will not deserve to be heard. He had entered the temple with his neck bowed by the weight of his sins, and, his eyelids pressed down by the heavy sickness of iniquity, he did not dare to look at heaven; timid, he draws his step back, and places himself last not so much in position as by the judgement of conscience; nor, ready in boldness, does he irreverently urge his foot forward to supplicate, but rather withdraws his steps; making his shame public, he repeatedly recalls his guilty breast by striking it, and pounds his conscious heart with the admonition of his fist. Not words but groans were heard from his mouth; and the whole confession was performed in only five words. The Lord makes this plain in the Gospel, that two men went up into the temple to pray: one was a Pharisee, and the other a publican; and the Pharisee, standing, prayed thus within himself, saying: God, I give you thanks, because I am not like other men, unjust, robbers, adulterers, as also this publican. I fast twice a week, I give tithes of all that I possess. But the publican stood far off, and would not even raise his eyes to heaven, but struck his breast, saying: God, be merciful to me a sinner (Luke 18:10 ff.). But notice what reverent supplication obtained from the searcher of the heart: shame, with a generous reward, found God, whom it desired to have merciful. And at once shame earned justification, which was proved in humility confessed, the Lord saying: I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than that Pharisee; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted (ibid., 14).

CHAPTER XVII. Then where do you place the example of that sinful woman, who is seen to have set out her crimes not in words but in tears? Though her tongue was silent in praying, she confessed [the secrets] of her conscience through the duty of penance. For the Lord was reclining in the house of a certain Pharisee, and that man had prepared a passing banquet for him as for a man invited. Learning of this, the prostitute boldly enters the Pharisee's house, and stands at the feet of the reclining Lord; she washes the holy footprints with tears, wipes them with her hair, kisses his soles unceasingly, and moistens his feet with precious ointment, and with almost all the limbs with which she had sinned before, she was expiating the stains of her crimes. Then the Lord, before whom our bones are laid apart, as the prophet says: All my bones shall say, Lord, who is like you (Ps. 34:10)?, lashes the murmur of the disparaging Pharisee. He praises with a wonderful proof the woman's hidden thought but manifest faith, and prefers the service of the one confessing to the preparations of the host, delighted more by the woman's deed than by the meal; for to him it was more to be delighted by conversion than to be fed, so that he who was not at all led by desire for food might be fed by the feast of confession. Do you see, he says, this woman? I entered your house; you did not give me a kiss, or water for my feet; but she, from the time she came in, has not ceased to kiss my feet. You did not anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with ointment. Therefore I tell you, her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much. And turning to the woman he said: Your sins are forgiven you (Luke 7:45 ff.). Is this small? But afterwards see what she hears: Daughter, your faith has made you safe; go in peace. Lately a sinner, soon released as a daughter, she who was laid waste by the war of her crimes is at once sent away released in the peace of the Lord. This is that prophetic oracle: When you have turned and groaned, then you will be saved; and: Tell your iniquities first, that you may be justified (Isa. 43:26). Since, then, you recognise by so many and such proofs that [God] delights in the sacrifice of penance, and you need not fear that the reward of a contrite heart and a humbled spirit will perish before the merciful judge, as Scripture says: A troubled spirit is a sacrifice to God; a contrite and humbled heart God does not despise (Ps. 50:19), why do you not hasten to emerge from the depth of luxury and from the whirlpool of worldly pleasure, and to breathe again from drunken deeds so as to take up the duties of penance? And do not think that, because you have distanced yourself from him, his ear is therefore closed to you: as soon as you knock, he will open the doors, and in pity he will shut you, pitiable one, within the enclosure of his court; only let him be moved by the complaint of your grief! The farther you had withdrawn, the more swiftly he will draw near, as the prophet says: God is near to the troubled in heart, and he will save the humble in spirit (Ps. 33:19). Of these the Lord says in the Gospel: Blessed, he says, are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted (Matt. 5:4).

CHAPTER XVIII. But perhaps penance seems harsh to you after the pleasures of the world. It is true; I perceive the defect of your health, I see the disease of your mind; but if you wish to be cured, do not heed the force of the treatment, and do not dread the remedy; when he applies the knife to your wound, the cure by cutting is made swifter. For the diligence of healing is worst handled when the festering sore is not cut away at once. The taste of the antidote is bitter, but what is unpleasant to the throat is life-giving and healthful. The Lord does not treat us as outsiders; he does not keep as strangers to himself whatever offenders he has healed. Every hour, every day intent on curing, he is neither held back by time nor hindered by any obstacles of delay. Plainly his power is hindered only when no one is found to be cured; for the Lord's kindness must lie idle when there is no one on whom he ought to have mercy. The chastisement of penance is harsh, but it is made gentler if the measure of the fault is weighed. Long ago the ambition of worldly pomp delighted you, and the dominion of the world claimed you as its slave, now relaxed in luxury, now sunk in drunkenness. Some saw you lately intent on the practice of the gambler, others [given] to dancing, others thrown upon a harlot; these saw you enslaved to brothels, smeared with ointments, anointed with spices, and dyed with foreign [colours]. You shone in garments, you gleamed with gold, you were adorned with gems and most precious pearls. Give back, then, turn for turn, and at least late render a recompense of times for times: divide your life reciprocally between both courses with equal measure. You belonged then to the devil; belong now to God; indeed rather belong now to yourself, who long were another's. And perhaps, if you consider, you have squandered much time, so that a short time confines what remains. Give yourself now to yourself, not to the times; give yourself to God, not to grow sluggish but to apply yourself to the business of confession. Return to the way from whose paths you had strayed, condemn what you had done, seek what you had been. First find yourself, that you may find what you seek; and if you find yourself, seek nothing apart from yourself. Put on sackcloth, sprinkle ashes, always pray in fasting, fast in prayer. These things by which the body is afflicted are the more precious, so that the beauty of the soul may be restored. A humble garment is rough, but what does not displease God is very becoming; the care of the body is mean, but it is itself the chief adornment of holiness. And do you still perhaps complain of the unworthiness of the clothing, you who have lost the wedding tunic? And though you appear disfigured by the nakedness of your foulness, do you not consider how you may be clothed again? Do you not fear, I ask, that with him who was called and entered the royal supper, you may be driven from the banquet of those reclining, reproached with a like condemnation, and hear it said to you: Friend, how did you come in here, not having a wedding garment (Matt. 22:12)? And when you find no argument to excuse yourself, he may say: Take him, with hands and feet bound, and cast him into the outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth (ibid., 13). And certainly that man is said to have been cast out because he had not sought or received [the garment]; for being called he entered, but reclined unclothed. If then he who never had it went out in this way because he did not seek it, how will he then be punished who received the tunic, and lost it, and could not be clothed again?

CHAPTER XIX. But, I suppose, you doubt that a lost garment can be sought again, or think it may be refused when you ask by him who lately gave it. Look in the Gospel at the younger son, begging after losing his inheritance, brought so far that under the pressure of want he wished to be a keeper of swine (Luke 15:15 ff.). He, worn out with utmost poverty and want, since he was not allowed even to feed on the swine's fodder, returned to the former soundness of his own mind and began to burn with longing for his earlier life, and, thinking of the abundance of his father's house, to condemn his guilt by the reproof of conversion. Having at last deliberated on penance, and having spoken with himself in the secret of his heart about satisfaction, he returns, as by right of homecoming, naked and an exile, to his father's hearth. Then that father, who had seen the plan in the heart of the one pondering it, before the lost son could pour out words in confession, anticipates the feeling of the grieving one, and mercifully receives him as he returns. He falls on his neck, reconciles him with kisses, and the father wonderfully strengthens him, still trembling and saying nothing. But that most prudent penitent and excellent confessor, secure of his father's wish yet still doubtful of his own satisfaction, sets out the order of confession he had meditated, and unfolds in words what he had turned over in his heart: Father, he says, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me as one of your hired servants (Luke 15:21). The father, therefore, appeased by the prayers of the one confessing, orders the first robe to be brought, and at once commands the naked one to be clothed with the garment lately lost. He orders a ring also to be given, restores the seal of the token, encloses his feet with the protection of shoes, and for his restoration orders the fattened calf to be killed, that is, he commands a most pleasing sacrifice to be offered for the reconciled one, which would be acceptable both to heaven and to the hosts of angels. A harsher obstinacy had roused the elder son to hatred of his brother; reproaching the crimes of the one received back, he objects. The command is not revoked, the father's kindness is not changed; he is declared his brother, he is called son; and he who had perfect counsel in repenting drew upon himself the full affection of the father. I was gladdened, he says, and rejoiced, because this your brother was dead, and has come to life again; he was lost, and is found (ibid., 24). You see, then, that for the converted son the former robe was restored by the purchase of penance, and that the father celebrated with every wish the return of the one confessing. For the lost inheritance signifies the sacrament of baptism, in which all the buildings of the heavenly kingdoms are established. This that son, that is, the faithful Christian who had obtained the freedom of the Father, had lost through the contagion of lust and luxury, and, set far from his God, had polluted himself with shameful deeds in utter foulness, and, enslaved to the devil, to whom he had given himself by a most abandoned way of life, he began to keep swine, that is, unclean spirits; and since he was not permitted to feed on their food, because by reason of the flesh he could not gorge himself on the demonic husks, deserted on both sides and destitute everywhere, he toiled, exhausted by want of good fruit.
