But having returned, he at once received all that he had been deprived of, and, restored to concord with the father, remained in the substance of his former possession. Return, then, you also, brother, return, and come to life from the dead, and be restored from the lost.

CHAPTER XX. — The good shepherd seeks his straying sheep, and rejoices more over the one found than over those not lost. He carries it back on his shoulders, puts it back in the company of his flock, and shuts it within the lodging of its former security; nor does he consider the number of those left behind, he who sought to complete the full hundred by recovering the one that was lost. A woman searches earnestly for a lost drachma: she lights a lamp, sweeps the house clean with brooms, and invites her friends and neighbours alike to rejoice over the drachma that was found. And does anyone think that God does not rejoice at the restoration of one who is converted, when he sees that the parable is fitted especially to the person of the penitent, as he himself says: I tell you, so there will be joy before the angels of God over one sinner doing penance (ibid., 10)? Consider, finally, that singular saying of the Lord, in which he said: Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are ill; for I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to penance (Matt. 9:12). The Lord therefore calls sinners to penance, and our physician wishes to benefit the sick more than the healthy. But he does not pass over the righteous because he takes sinners to himself: for the life of the righteous is the divine calling, just as he who searched for the one straying sheep left the ninety-nine on the mountains, intending to render to these the reward due to righteousness, and to confer on that one the benefit of mercy. The Apostle proves this, saying: But to him who does not work, and believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned as righteousness, according to the purpose of the grace of God (Rom. 4:5). Then hear with what darts the Lord strikes the hearts of sinners in the Gospel, and you will understand how highly he valued the sacrament of penance. There were present, it says, some who told him about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices. Then Jesus said: Do you think that these Galileans were sinners beyond the Galileans, because they suffered such things? I tell you, unless you do penance, you will all likewise perish (Luke 13:3 ff.). Or those eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them, do you think that they were sinners beyond the others who lived in Jerusalem? I tell you, unless you do penance, you will all likewise perish. And to prove the matter he added the example of a comparison, making mention of a fig tree which, barren and fruitless, is ordered to be cut down; but at the intercession of the vinedresser its destruction is allowed to be deferred, so that, dug around with fitting cultivation and a basket of dung applied, it may be given time to bring forth the fruits of penance. Further, if a tree that produced no fruit of its kind was ordered to be cut down before its time, with what iron must the trunk be hewn that, overgrown with briars and choked with alien thorns, received no cultivation for its restoration? For the likeness of the tree is an example of the faithful man who, empty of the fruit of his faith, has given no thought to anything that would profit him toward the gain of future hope; for it had been planted in a vineyard, and that vineyard signifies especially the Church, in which that tree had been planted; but by the dresser of this vineyard the person of the priest seems to be expressed, who works the trench of the unfruitful plant with the cultivation of the Lord's precepts; and by the basket of dung the duty of penance is signified. But if, after the delay of time, fruit could not be found on it at all, it would wither, torn up by the roots in the future, that is, cut down at the future judgement, it would burn like the useless, discarded material of timber, made fodder for the eternal fire; although this may also be understood both of Christ and of the Jewish people.

CHAPTER XXI. — I believe that by these proofs, which we have brought forth abundantly with zeal, out of [your] infirmities, to raise and rouse your mind, it has become sufficiently clear to your understanding that God, the fountain of mercy, does not will the destruction of sinners, but rather wishes to have the wrongdoer corrected, so that however many offences are counted, so great should be the work of penance. Let him not despair of a swift restoration through his return, who hears the Lord himself urging penance on the sinner. This the Apocalypse of the most blessed John sets out more expressly, in which he rebukes the angels of the Churches, so that, cheated by their former errors, they may bow down to the laments of penance; for so the Lord is shown to desire the ruin of no one, since he presses penance on the one who falls. To the angel of the Church of Ephesus, then, he says: Remember from where you have fallen, and do penance, and do the first works; but if not, I am coming to you, and will move your lampstand from its place, unless you do penance (Apoc. 2:5). And yet behold, he is called an angel, to whom the care of penance and conversion is entrusted, and he is urged to accomplish his former works, so that it may be made known to him that he has lost nothing of all his merits. Yet the admonition threatens more gravely the one who does not do penance, if he persists in the stubbornness of the hardened; for the severity of punishment will be inexcusable if the first correction has not bent the untamed neck; and he will perish by his own evil who, forewarned by the authority of the one who threatens, does not submit his obstinate neck to the yoke of satisfaction. He declares that the man will surely return to his former state who is corrected by the fitting humility of confession so as to run the course of the true life. This is declared more fully a little later, when the angel of the Church of Thyatira is chastised with the lash of rebuke. I have, he says, many things against you, because you tolerate the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess, and teaches and seduces my servants to commit fornication and to eat of things sacrificed to idols. And I gave her time to do penance, and she would not repent of her fornications; and I will cast her into a bed, and those who commit adultery with her will be in great tribulation, unless they do penance for all their deeds; and I will kill her children with the sword; and all the Churches shall know that I am the searcher of heart and reins, who render to each according to his deeds (Apoc. 2:20). What indeed could be said more humane, what more merciful? And I gave her, he says, time to do penance, and she would not repent. You have nothing, sinner, you have nothing to excuse yourself with: there is no reason for you to doubt with cause, no reason to despair without cause; gird yourself with these examples for confessing, arm yourself with these proofs for penance.

CHAPTER XXII. — For the Lord defers punishment so that he may find penance; and using delaying intervals, he prolongs his patience, so that clemency may not lose what ought to have been done by censure. He does not look at past evils, nor count errors, but praises what is corrected. You have the promise of him who urges you to penance; if you do not repent, he will charge it to you: And I gave her, he says, time to do penance, and she would not repent. Like this is that prophetic word: And he said, after she had committed all these fornications: Return to me; and she would not return to me (Jer. 3:7). But if, driven round by the enormity of your crimes, you cast yourself into the whirlpool of despair, or, with checked step, hesitate to root out the heap [that blocks] your way, or, sliding further through the lapse of a perverse mind, you lead your feet, as they incline downward, in a slippery course, at once the hope of recovery, once lost, is taken from you; the gulf of [your] deeds will seize you, swallowing [you] into the abyss; your eyes will be closed by the night of sin, so that they may not see the flashing ray of the true light; the blindness of death will set itself against [you], and the deceiving angels will lead you round, here and there, as if in some game. All outrages will become pleasing to you, and the licence to sin will thoroughly delight you; the devil will hold you, bound over to him under the hope of freedom, so that you are free to sin, not to live. Nor will he let you look back to what you were before, once, most seductive as he is, he has lured you away with the allurement of sinning and the sweetness of crimes; and, to put it once for all, he will so deceive you with the sweetness of perishing that it will seem more delightful to you to perish than to return. For no sin is committed without its own delight, nor can it ensnare the mind otherwise than by enticing with the sweetness of desire the one it has deceived; for the deadly preparation of a lethal cup must be a sweet mixture and pleasant to the throat, lest the first taste of bitterness call back the one drinking. So, indeed, the poison of that tree seemed to the first woman good to look at and sweet to eat; and after its sweetness had lied to the lips of the one eating, the violent subtlety of the draught infected the one dying, extinguished what remained vigorous and lively; and, her desires falling back into their opposite through intemperance, it cast [her] out from the paradise of blessedness and the estate of security into the exile of the world and the spectacle of the age.

CHAPTER XXIII. — I beg you, brother, fear these things, flee them and dread them; and do not allow the enemy to rejoice over your perdition and to raise a victor's brow in the sight of God. Beware the return of the seven unclean spirits, to whom the leader of all evils joined himself as an eighth. And since no one can endure one devil, who could bear the dominion of eight? As the Lord says: When the unclean spirit has gone out of a man, he passes through waterless places, seeking rest, and not finding it, he says: I will return to my house from which I came out; and returning he finds it empty, swept with brooms, and set in order. Then he goes and brings with him seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and they enter and dwell there; and the last state of that man becomes worse than the first (Matt. 12:43). If a hostile band had taken you, hemmed in by a warlike siege, and the hand of a plunderer had held you captive in a barbarian raid, what tears would you shed, what wailing would you utter, what laments would you pour out? You would sigh all day and night, you would not seek food, you would not desire drink; you would be drained and wasted by hunger, only the dryness of rough skin and a wrinkled leanness would appear in you; your hair would stiffen, matted with filth, and the shaggy locks of your squalid head, and your limbs, pressed by a long beard, would bristle; you would hand over your inheritance for a ransom under the sword; you would walk bound, naked, poor and stripped of everything; you would have sought to escape, and if a way of flight were offered, you would ponder, uncertain, how to overcome the danger at the greatest risk. The author of crimes holds you captive; he keeps you bound not with iron bonds but with the chains of crimes; he has put the fetters of lust on you, and hemmed you in on every side with a stricter guard; he has given you a law, that you should think everything lawful that is not lawful; he has sunk you alive in the pit of eternal death; and do you not understand the loss of your salvation, the forfeiture of eternal hope, and the ruin of perpetual life? You go about adorned with finery of garments, you celebrate meals with sumptuous foods, you are soaked with wine, you fatten your soul with daily feasts, you never cease to cultivate the enormous gluttony of your body, to say nothing meanwhile of other crimes. Do you think, do you really think, that this too is not of divine punishment, that you do not know how you ought to repent of your crimes? As the Apostle proves, who says: Because they did not have God in their knowledge, he gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do what is not fitting (Rom. 1:28); and again: Because they did not receive the love of truth, that they might be saved, God sent them the working of error, that all may be judged who did not believe the truth (2 Thess. 2:10). Of such men, finally, he fears that, coming to Corinth, he may mourn many of those who have not done penance for the uncleanness which they committed, and for fornications and lust (2 Cor. 12:21).

CHAPTER XXIV. Think of that rich man's sumptuous dinners and the rich abundance of his plentiful feasts, wrapped in purple of the richer murex and in the woven sheen of silk, all his thought on the hope of the present time, none on the future. Hear what was laid up for him after all these things. After purple, flame; after feasts, want, so that he who had once drunk deep of precious nectar begged for a little drop of water, and asked, yet did not receive, the comfort of a wet fingertip from the one to whom in the world he had refused the crumbs of his feasts. Confess, I beg you, all the things of which you remember yourself guilty; confess, and come before the face of God with the duty of satisfaction; humble your heart before him, and bow your neck in his sight; bend your knees, and lay yourself on the ground with your face pressed down. That heavenly advocate will at once take up your groaning, and will not fail to intercede for you with his Father, he who is accustomed to give faithful patronage to penitents. He will not plead his case with arguments according to a prescribed kind of eloquence, but will at once obtain the benefit of pardon, he who expects no fee from the one he has won. The Apostle proves this, saying: Who shall bring an accusation against God's elect? It is God who justifies; who is it that condemns? Christ who died, yes, and who also rose again, who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us (Rom. 8:33). In agreement, the most blessed apostle John sets down in his epistle and says: If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us; but if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just, to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity. If we say that we do not sin, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us. My little children, I write these things to you so that you may not sin; and if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus, and he pleads for our sins (1 John 1:8 ff.). All that the Son of God, the Lord Jesus Christ, who is the way, the truth and the life, has spoken is law; and he taught by his example that what he commanded us in writing should be done; for he would not want anything done by us which he himself had not done, or which would not please him when we do it. Nor could what he himself had commanded displease him, since he who commanded it had first done it himself. For the teaching of a command would be empty if the authority of the teacher's deed did not go before it; but whatever the Lord commanded, he also did, and what he commanded to be done in imitation of himself will not be empty. The same Lord, then, set these things before his disciples to keep: Take heed to yourselves: if your brother sins against you, forgive him; and if he sins against you seven times in a day, and seven times turns back to you saying, I repent, forgive him, and it will be forgiven you (Luke 17:3). And when he was consulted on the matter by the holy apostle Peter, who said: Lord, if my brother sins against me, how often shall I forgive him? Up to seven times? Jesus said to him: I do not say to you up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven (Matt. 18:21). He, then, who commands us to forgive seven times the debts of a brother who sins against us, does he not keep the form of his command toward us? Or he who said: I desire mercy more than sacrifice (Hos. 6:6), can he deny us the treasure of mercy? This would be, if I may say it having first begged pardon, to believe that the Lord Jesus lied in all that he taught, if he were unwilling to keep toward us the form of his own commands.

CHAPTER XXV. And it is well that he at once fits to this saying, by way of comparison, the parable of the two servants, of whom one, when on account of a great debt, his money spent, he was ordered to be sold together with his wife and children, and falling at his lord's feet he begged his patience, that, being granted time, he would repay the whole debt, and he obtained by his lord's mercy that everything was forgiven him: this man, who on such terms had been held condemned to torments, himself would not have mercy on his fellow servant who was his debtor; because he forgot the kindness very lately granted to him, he is at once handed over to the torturers, and the same [debt] that had a little before been forgiven is exacted from his blood. Hence it is that the Lord laid down this order of praying, saying: And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors (Matt. 6:12); so that you may know that as much can be forgiven you as you have forgiven your own debtor; indeed, that you may be seen to spare yourself when, being entreated, you pardon another. For you will without doubt be judged by your own judgement if, wanting to be forgiven yourself, you are unwilling to forgive another, as the Lord says: With what judgement you judge, with the same you will be judged; and with what measure you measure, with the same it will be measured back to you (Matt. 7:2). I want you to read more attentively the beginning of the prophet Zechariah, and there you will find that by which you may be more strongly encouraged. The Lord, he says, was angry with our fathers with great anger (Zech. 1:2). Who, hearing this, would not tremble? Who, terrified by the thunder of this voice, would not wither? Or what mind would this declared indignation not disturb? For what state of soundness could be kept where so vehement an anger of the Creator was proclaimed? And it was not enough to have said anger, unless it was also declared great, as if, were it not great, even his milder wrath could be endured. But let us see what outcome so great a commotion announces. I suppose, [you think,] he said: I will trouble you with the tumults of war, punish you with the cruel dominion of captivity, afflict you with famine, shake you with disease, consume you with death; the unforeseen ravaging of wild beasts and animals will seize you; exile will drive you about as fugitives scattered everywhere. For this is left to the understanding, that a more vehement vengeance should follow great anger. The Lord, he says, was angry with our fathers with great anger, saying to them (Zech. 1:2). Let us hear what he said: Turn to me, and I will turn to you. O indignation flowing from tenderness! O great anger, which brings in mercy! I ask, he who is angry in this way, how does he show mercy? Or if he shows mercy in this way, how is he angry when indignant? Another prophet declares this: Return, Israel, to your Lord, because you have grown weak in your iniquities. Say to him: You are able to forgive our sins, not that you may receive iniquity, but that you may receive good things; and render to him the fruit of your lips, and your heart will feast on good things (Hos. 14:2); and elsewhere: Return, he says, deserting sons, says the Lord (Isa. 46:8); and again: Return, returning sons, and I will heal your affliction (Jer. 3:22). In harmony with these, blessed David sang the comforts of sinners, saying: Confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is for ever (Ps. 105:1).

CHAPTER XXVI. Nor would I say this so as to seem to have given too loose a rein to licence, and, under pretext of a pardon to be granted by God, to have made penance rather a kindling of sin for its author; for by this discourse of mine I raise up the one who is falling, I do not push the one who is standing; nor do I prejudge innocence when I exhort the sinner to penance. For, as we have already said above, innocence claims from God the reward owed to its life, while penance awaits the benefit of mercy; for not to sin is to fear, but to repent is more than to fear. For carefree prosperity is often exposed to offences, while he whom fear corrects becomes more cautious in avoiding past things; because he will always be more anxious who takes care not to fall again where he has already fallen before. So dangers experienced make a helmsman anxious, and he who has even once suffered shipwreck through carelessness is sometimes afraid to enter harbours of which he has had no ill experience. Accordingly, divine Scripture says: He who has not been tempted, what does he know (Ecclus. 34:9)? to show that through the occasion of temptation the one tempted is always made more cautious, and he who was before heedless is corrected more through fear by the knowledge of temptation. And the Lord so desires to pardon sinners, he who does not wish the death of the one dying so much as that he should turn back and live, that those whom he sometimes appoints to punishment for their crimes he hastens at once to absolve when entreated by penance; and, to put the sword back in its sheath, he changes the sentence of punishment in return for satisfaction.

CHAPTER XXVII. And although this has been proved above from the deed of the Ninevites, nevertheless take also the testimony of the prophet Jeremiah on it, so that the example may be proved to you more fully by testimonies. The word, he says, which came from the Lord to Jeremiah, saying: Arise, and go down to the potter's house, and there you will hear my words. And I went down to the potter's house, and behold, he was doing his work on the stones, and the vessel which he was making in his hands fell; and again he made it into another vessel, as it pleased him to make. And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Shall I not be able to do with you as this potter, house of Israel? Behold, as the potter's clay you are in my hands; and if I speak against a nation or against a kingdom, to remove them and destroy them, and if that nation turns from its evil thoughts, I will repent of the evils which I thought to do to them, and I will not do them. And yet if I speak about a kingdom or a nation, that it be built up and planted round about, and it does wickedness in my sight, so as not to hear my voice, I will repent of the good things which I spoke of doing to them, and I will not do them. And now say to the men of Judah and those living in Jerusalem: Behold, I am fashioning evils against you and devising a device against you. Let each one turn from his wicked way; make your thoughts better (Jer. 18:1 ff.). Our potter, then, urges us to turn away from the worst ways and from wicked thoughts, so that the conversion of penance may mould our cracks and flaws into another vessel. And he wishes the substance of his work not to perish, [but to come] to penance, so that the sentence may not hold as guilty one whom confession excuses. With this agrees the Wisdom of Solomon: But you have mercy, Lord, he says, on all, because you can do all things, and you overlook the sins of men for the sake of penance; for power is at hand for you when you will, and since you are Lord of all, you make yourself spare all (Wis. 11:24). Let us therefore turn and confess to the Lord while we pass our time in this furlough of the world, and let us prepare for our judge the provision of penance. Let the courses of our time not be idle, and let us not live as men born to sin, but to do good. Or if we have become liable to sin, since in this theatre of the world it cannot be that we do not sin, let us remember ourselves, so that we may desire to escape the precipice of hell. Let us therefore repent from faith, pray from the heart, weep from our inmost being. And as the Prophet says: Let us worship and fall down and weep before the Lord who made us; for those who sow in tears will reap in joy (Ps. 94:6). Happy, ah, too happy the office of tears, by which rewards are gathered in the time to come! And blessed the increase of the seed which is poured out in weeping, that it may be reaped in gladness! For it is written: Happy the man who recognises his own wailing. Let us lift up our eyes to the mountains, from where help will come to us; for as the eyes of servants are on the hands of their masters, and as the eyes of a maidservant on the hands of her mistress, so also our eyes are on the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us (Ps. 122:2).

CHAPTER XXVIII.—Nor let us so prolong the resolve of our conversion for the delights of the moment that, knowing we sin and delighting in perishing, we plunge ourselves into a whirlpool of crimes right up to extreme old age; since it is held uncertain what end may close the use of life conferred on us by divine favour. And perhaps what is thought either the first or the middle [part of life] already marks the goal of an imminent setting, and the due end may be the summons of a Lord made indignant by the slowness of our conversion; since indeed an oracle seems to have been set forth to warn us to break off delays in conversion: Do not be slow to turn to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day; for his anger comes suddenly, and in the time of vengeance he will destroy you (Ecclus. 5:8); and again: Son, you have sinned; do not add [to it] again, but pray also about the former [sins], that they may be forgiven you; and do not add sin upon sin and say: The compassion of God is great; for mercy and anger are from him (Ecclus. 21:1). Nor let us suffer ourselves to become slaves until death, and give our bodies into the power of crimes, but let us obey the Apostle who says: Let not sin reign in your mortal body, so that you obey it (Rom. 6:12); so that, since sins cannot be absent, at least they may not reign, that is, that there may not be an unbridled licence for sinning with no regard for escaping. Or indeed, if anyone thinks that time remains to him for sinning, and that when his lust is sated, when the strength of the body has already ruled over the mind, he may then return to the decision to repent, let him declare to me the last time of his life: by whose reckoning he has learned it, by whose suggestion he has come to know it; so that he may rightly, so to speak, flatter himself about the span of time. But since our final departure is unforeseen, and the course of our life is doubtful through ignorance of death, how does anyone think time remains to him for confessing, who does not know the time of his own time, when he surely hears Scripture saying: Living and in health you will confess, and you will praise God, and you will go into the portion of the holy age with the living and those who give confession (Ecclus. 17:27)? For delay should create time for confession, and not breed despair; for damnation is heaped up by delay for him who presumes upon the divine patience with stubborn boldness. This is shown to have come to pass in the times of holy Noah, when patience, drawn out through a hundred years, poured an implacable flood over the circuit of the world, as judgement overflowed. Hence the blessed Apostle says: Or do you despise the riches of his goodness and his long patience, not knowing that the goodness of God leads you to penance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart you store up for yourself wrath on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the just judgement of God, who will render to each according to his deeds (Rom. 2:4).

CHAPTER XXIX.—I want you to tell me what is the glory of present things, what are the fruits of this time, what the use of perishable things. The power of a kingdom, as I have said, is ended by death; the ambition of authority is cut off by succession; abundance of riches is often withdrawn from us while we live; the enjoyment of pleasure is spoiled when sadness intervenes; the delight of joys is violated by the dread of fear; and everything that is seized by desire, whatever the body or the soul of the body desires, is cut down by the sickle of the end. Nor can anything obtain the perfect privilege of blessedness which the infinity of eternity does not surround; for that must be perishable which is measured by inevitable necessity: that whose life a chance event sometimes cuts off will without doubt remain liable, inconstant and weak. Since all these things, then, are ended by death, what is our own in death itself? If we have nothing by which conscience is burdened with the increase of good work; and if we have been able to have nothing good of our own, what shall we carry with us as we return to our homeland? How naked and misshapen will our soul remain, if we do not at least cover it with the veils of penance and the garments of confession! unless it be that we hasten to hide our disgrace, and do not strive to cover the nakedness of the soul; whose beauty is by nature invisible, but whose deformity from the filth of sins will become visible.

CHAPTER XXX.—Those are the dealings to be taken up, those the riches to be embraced, that the power to be sought, which time does not snatch away, place does not withdraw, no person takes off; which remains in a perpetual state, which is kept by an eternal privilege, which is not withdrawn by an end, which is neither pressed nor driven by the yoke of death. For there the goods of conscience are safe, where it will no longer be possible to sin after the present evils of the world, where the devil has no access, where there is no place for darkness; but neither is there found at all anyone who deceives, nor anyone who can be deceived. There all good things, there all happy things, there all prosperity: no day will appear changeable by increase of light, no sun slower in rising, brighter in shining, dimmer in setting; night will be wholly absent, there will be no moon, nor will the twinkling of the stars glow more fiercely; no one will feel hunger, tears will be wiped away, no fear, dread from nothing, delight [will be] all things, peace the whole, and joy will possess whatever had been liable to sadness. The prophet Isaiah sets out all things clearly (Isa. 60:2 ff.). What glory of the happy will there be there then, what punishments of the wretched, what groans, what sighs of sinners, what blessedness of the saints? For these, fellowship with God; for those, to be given over to the torment of the flames of hell: these to enjoy incomparable refreshment, those to be slaughtered by unquenchable fire: these, unwearied, to be delighted by the springs of paradise and the tops of the groves and by streams, those, beset by a pool of fire and a stream of burning and the darkness of black night, to be pressed hard by inescapable punishments: in the end, these to enjoy heavenly goods, those to be consumed by the devouring of all hell and of eternal death?

CHAPTER XXXI.—If now, as far as this world goes, someone undone by the blight of poverty does not have at hand anything with which to sustain his starving hunger with any sort of food, and sees another load his tables with rich dishes, and, stuffed with feasts, drink from jewels, and draw out at length, with ostentatious display, banquets spiced with foreign flavours, what sighs do you think he draws from the deepest part of his inner being, what complaints his bowels utter in pain; sometimes even shedding tears, when he begins to be seized a little more by desire for the things seen, and feels an ineffectual desire burning more and more out of desire? What then will be the groans of the unhappy, what torment will arise by that comparison with inconsolable grief, when they see the host of happy souls enjoying heavenly abundance and everlasting riches, and themselves cheated of a drop from a moistened finger, and enduring besides an unquenchable flame, when they are kept with no hope of pardon? We cannot bear the heat of the sun, we barely tolerate the heat of the baths, we feel the blaze of furnaces and withdraw far off; who will bear the surging hell, and who will be able to endure the roar of the smoking abyss seething with the furnaces of Tartarus, and sustain the masses of infernal darkness; where only the howling of the burning is heard, and the wailing of the cruelly punished resounds? These things, I pray, how they are to be fled, how guarded against, and avoided with all our strength and all our soul and mind!

CHAPTER XXXII.—Since, then, the gates of pardon lie open, since the harbour of penance is offered to those tossed and driven by the storm of crimes, since a cure is promised to sick minds, and a willing physician pledges medicine and life to the wounded: since mercy is at hand, before justice draws the dagger out to the hilt, let us take up the arms of penance and soften the judge's severity by the duty of satisfaction. For he holds the gift of pardon as certain who is permitted to repent; for without doubt he is not allowed to confess for whom no tenderness is kept. This is proved by the condemnation of the ancient serpent at the very origin of the world, whom the thunderbolt of the sentence struck down unheard, and whom unrelenting severity cast out, unentreated, from the possession of his state. This the regions of Sodom and Gomorrah, burned up by heavenly fire, attest, for which, because of the excess of their crimes, nothing was reserved for penance, lest perhaps, having been warned, they might avoid the justice of vengeance. This the destruction of Pharaoh in Exodus cries out, this the unexpected end of Korah, Dathan and Abiram bears witness to, this the punishments of Antiochus and Herod declare, this the shipwreck of Ananias and Sapphira by sudden punishment shows: whom vengeance did not put off to the present time, and, pardon being denied, severity accompanying [it] cut them down. Let not the day of departure find us unprepared, nor the time of that winter or sabbath shut us within the devil's camp. Let us keep watch against the deceitful snares and open threats of the ancient enemy; for he is roused more fiercely against those who have turned, and pursues his deserters more severely, as if mocked. Then, when he was deceiving, he had lured with blandishments; now he troubles with temptations and cruelties: then he had been as a friend, now he rages as an enemy; and by the fall he has made the one he dashed down more cautious, but the one dashed down sometimes dashes down the one who dashed him. Let us flee the showy allurements of the world, and give its ambitions a complete divorce. This the apostle John urges, saying: Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him; for all that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, and the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the age, which is not from the Father, but is from the desire of the world: and the world will pass away, and its desire. But he who does the will of God remains for ever, as God also remains for ever (1 John 2:15). Let us be washed with the baptism of penance, so that we may see the Lord with a pure heart: let us remove wickedness from our souls, from the sight of God's eyes, let us learn to do justice; let us seek judgement, rescue the one suffering wrong, judge for the orphan, vindicate the widow, and we shall reason with the Lord. And if our sins are like scarlet, he will make them white as snow; and if like crimson, he will make them like white wool. And because he will sprinkle with hyssop and we shall be cleansed, he will wash us and we shall be whiter than snow (Ps. 50:9).

CHAPTER XXXIII. There are three things which the Lord, having established them by his own will, maintains towards us: I mean goodness, mercy, and justice. Goodness is that by which we have come to be; mercy, that by which we are called to penance; justice, that by which we shall be judged in time to come. These meanwhile keep within themselves the order of times, past, present, and future: the past, in which by the Lord's authorship we are created and born; the present, in which, being converted, we earn mercy; the future, in which we shall be rewarded according to our works, as justice apportions. Therefore, since we hold the kingdom of mercy in our hands, and the gifts of loving-kindness are placed within our choice, let us here cleanse our consciences from all defilement, and from now on fit ourselves, by good conduct, with spiritual instruments. Let us shun the desires that war against our souls, and let us in no way tolerate a profane conscience. We shall obtain all that we believe by faith, if we order ourselves by righteous acts in a blameless life. We shall earn the remission of all sins, we shall rise again to eternal life in the resurrection of believers; and, if boldness may presume to speak further, we shall enter the kingdom of heaven with the righteous, with whom we have earned a share through penance, as Scripture says: But to the penitent he gave a share of righteousness, and he exhorted those who were failing to endure, and he destined them for the lot of truth (Ecclus. 17).

These things, most beloved brother, by which I might exhort you, together with myself, to the practice of penance, I have written down, so far as the modesty of my ability could gather them from the readings of the Lord. If, as I think, you already follow them by zeal of mind and by your own resolve, and, seated in the chariot of confession, are making for pardon, take me with you as a partner in this thought, so that, joined in common company, we may hasten to the goal of indulgence: or if, hindered by the sluggishness of laziness, I cannot follow your swiftness, remember me; and when you have earned the reward from God's generosity, I beg that in your prayers you may by no forgetfulness let slip Victor.
